The company has said its ADMT is a security, fraud-prevention, or safety tool. That description alone does not take the system outside Article 11. The CPPA specifically considered, and rejected, a broader exemption for this category of tool. In its Final Statement of Reasons, the Agency explained that "the regulations already include appropriate exceptions for security, fraud prevention, and safety" — narrow, specific ones (11 CCR §§ 7220(d)(2), 7222(c)(2)) — and that a broader carve-out "would be less effective at protecting consumer privacy" because it would remove the risk-assessment, notice, and opt-out/access rights for decisions that otherwise qualify. If this tool's output is used to make a decision within one of § 7001(ddd)'s categories — for example, denying a transaction as fraudulent, which is a financial-services decision — labeling it a "security tool" does not, by itself, exempt it. Section 2 addresses whether the narrow, specific exceptions actually apply on this company's own facts. (California Privacy Protection Agency, Final Statement of Reasons, CCPA Updates, Cyber, Risk, ADMT, and Insurance Regulations, 11 CCR § 7001(ddd), Appendix p. 24.)
